title: Novo Nordisk Sues Eli Lilly Over Misleading GLP-1 Weight-Loss Drug Ads
excerpt: The Danish drugmaker accuses Eli Lilly of cherry-picking outdated clinical data to exaggerate the superiority of Zepbound over Wegovy, escalating a high-stakes battle in the nearly $100 billion obesity drug market.
body:
• Novo Nordisk filed a federal lawsuit against Eli Lilly in New Jersey on Tuesday, alleging its rival's direct-to-consumer ads for Zepbound and Mounjaro violate the Lanham Act and state unfair-competition laws.
  • The suit claims Lilly's TV commercials compare the highest doses of its drugs to lower doses of Novo's Wegovy and Ozempic, omitting newer, higher-dose formulations that show comparable weight loss.
  • Novo says Lilly's contested ad campaign has been served to consumers more than 700 million times since late April.
  • The GLP-1 obesity drug market is projected to exceed $100 billion in annual sales by 2030, with both companies racing to lock in patients.

Novo Nordisk sued Eli Lilly in U.S. District Court in New Jersey on Tuesday, accusing the American drugmaker of running a nationwide false advertising campaign that misleads patients about the relative effectiveness of their competing GLP-1 weight-loss and diabetes medications.

The complaint alleges Lilly violated federal and state false advertising and unfair competition laws, including the Lanham Act, through direct-to-consumer ads for its obesity drug Zepbound and diabetes treatment Mounjaro. At the center of the dispute is a television commercial in which Lilly claims people taking Zepbound lost an average of 50 pounds compared to 33 pounds for those on Wegovy.

The Dose Discrepancy

Novo says that comparison is fundamentally dishonest. The ads pit the highest approved dose of Zepbound against Wegovy's older, lower 2.4-milligram dose — while omitting that the FDA approved a higher 7.2-milligram dose of Wegovy in March 2026. In clinical trials, patients on that higher dose lost an average of 47 pounds, nearly matching the 48-pound average seen with Zepbound's top dose in separate late-stage trials.

"The ads are maliciously and deceptively false because Lilly knowingly cites outdated clinical trials that compare the highest doses of the Lilly medicines to lower doses of Novo Nordisk's medicines."

— Novo Nordisk, court complaint

Novo's general counsel John Kuckelman told Reuters the company sent Lilly a cease-and-desist letter in April, shortly after the FDA approved the higher Wegovy dose. Lilly did not respond to the letter, Kuckelman said. Instead, the company added what he described as an "inadequate disclaimer" — a text note acknowledging that a higher-dose version of Wegovy was not included in the study. Novo argues the disclaimer was far less prominent than the bold 50-versus-33-pound weight-loss comparison.

Scale of the Campaign

The lawsuit paints a picture of an advertising blitz of unusual scale. Novo says Lilly's contested ads have been served to consumers more than 700 million times just since the company modified them in late April. The suit also alleges Lilly used the "same misleading approach" in ads comparing its diabetes drug Mounjaro to Novo's Ozempic, citing higher-dose Mounjaro against lower-dose Ozempic even when a higher-dose version of Ozempic was available.

Novo is seeking a permanent injunction requiring Lilly to pull the ads, a court-ordered corrective advertising campaign, and damages including Lilly's profits attributable to the advertisements. The company has said it will seek a preliminary injunction if Lilly does not voluntarily remove the ads.

A Market at an Inflection Point

The legal battle arrives at a pivotal moment for the GLP-1 market. Analysts project the obesity drug sector will generate more than $100 billion in annual sales by 2030. Zepbound's sales alone reached nearly $4.2 billion in the first quarter of 2026, an 80 percent increase from the prior year.

Novo was first to market with injectable Wegovy but lost ground to Zepbound after Lilly's aggressive commercial push. Under new CEO Maziar Mike Doustdar, Novo has fought back with oral Wegovy, whose strong launch has held up even against Lilly's competing GLP-1 pill, Foundayo. The lawsuit is another sign of a more combative Novo — Doustdar also moved quickly to sue Hims & Hers Health earlier this year when it launched a compounded version of the Wegovy pill. That dispute was later settled through a distribution deal.

The competitive dynamics intensified further on July 1, when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services launched the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, opening coverage for weight-loss medications to millions of older Americans at a $50 monthly copay. Both companies stand to gain from the expanded patient pool, raising the stakes on which brand captures prescriber and patient loyalty.

Market Reaction

Shares of Eli Lilly fell 0.5 percent to $1,141.84 in pre-market U.S. trading on Tuesday, while Copenhagen-listed Novo Nordisk shares dropped 1.7 percent. Eli Lilly did not immediately respond to requests for comment from multiple news outlets.

The lawsuit underscores how the GLP-1 race has moved beyond the lab and the pharmacy counter into the courtroom, with hundreds of billions of dollars in future revenue hinging not just on clinical results but on how those results are presented to patients.
